trigger: A substring must satisfy a property for every character it contains, and a single bad character can never be inside any valid answer.
key_idea: Any character whose opposite case is absent can never be part of a nice substring, so it splits the problem: recurse on the left and right pieces and keep the longer.
approach: Build a set of characters present in the current string.
Scan for the first char whose swapped-case partner is missing.
If none is missing, the whole string is nice; return it.
Otherwise recurse on s[:i] and s[i+1:].
Return the longer result, preferring the left on ties.

complexity.time: O(n * 26) recursive splits, O(n^2) worst case

gotcha: Ties must return the earliest occurrence, so compare with >= in favor of the left half; also strings shorter than 2 can never be nice.

trigger: You need to know whether every letter of a fixed small alphabet appears at least once.
key_idea: Collect distinct letters into a set; the sentence is a pangram exactly when the set has 26 entries.
approach: Create an empty set.
Add every character of the sentence to it.
Return whether the set size equals 26.
gotcha: A 26-bit integer mask works too, but do not forget the input is guaranteed lowercase; mixed case would need normalization.

trigger: You can raise elements with a limited budget k and want the largest group made equal, which hints at a window over sorted values.
key_idea: After sorting, the best target for a window is its rightmost value; the window is valid when (length * nums[r]) - windowSum <= k.
approach: Sort nums and keep a running window sum.
Expand r one at a time, adding nums[r] to the sum.
While window_len * nums[r] > sum + k, shrink from the left.
Track the maximum window length seen.
Return that maximum.
gotcha: Use the running sum instead of recomputing, and note the window never needs to shrink below its previous best, so a non-shrinking window also works.

trigger: You need a statistic for every fixed-size window of an array, so recompute incrementally instead of from scratch.
key_idea: Maintain a frequency map for the current window; the distinct count is the map's size, updated by removing the outgoing element and adding the incoming one.
approach: Fill a frequency map with the first k elements.
Record its size as the first answer.
For each new index, decrement the outgoing element's count.
Delete the key when its count hits zero.
Increment the incoming element, append the map size.
gotcha: Forgetting to delete zero-count keys makes len(freq) overcount distinct elements.

trigger: Many intervals overlap a small bounded range of years and you need the point covered by the most intervals.
key_idea: Use a difference array: +1 at birth, -1 at death, then a running prefix sum gives the population of each year in order.
approach: Allocate an array covering years 1950 to 2050.
For each person add 1 at birth and subtract 1 at death.
Sweep years accumulating a running population.
Update the answer only on a strictly greater population.
Return the year with the first maximum.
gotcha: A person is not alive in their death year, so the -1 goes at death, not death + 1, and use strict > to keep the earliest year.

trigger: Repeatedly reducing the largest value to the next distinct value, so count how many steps each element must take.
key_idea: Each element must be reduced once per distinct value below it, so after sorting descending, every time the value changes, all elements seen so far need one more operation.
approach: Sort nums in descending order.
Keep a counter of elements processed so far.
Whenever nums[i] differs from nums[i-1], add the counter to the result.
Increment the counter for each element.
Return the result.
gotcha: Equal adjacent values do not add operations, so compare with the previous element rather than adding on every index.

trigger: Undirected graph given as an edge list and you must decide whether two vertices are connected.
key_idea: Build an adjacency list and traverse from source with a visited array; reaching destination means a path exists.
approach: Build an adjacency list from the edge list in both directions.
Push source on a stack and mark it seen.
Pop a node and iterate its neighbors.
Return true if a neighbor is destination; otherwise push unseen neighbors.
Return whether destination was seen after the loop.
gotcha: Handle source == destination, and mark nodes seen when pushed, not when popped, to avoid duplicate stack entries.

trigger: Asked for the greatest common divisor of two specific numbers derived from an array.
key_idea: Only min and max matter; the Euclidean algorithm gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) finds their GCD quickly.
approach: Find the minimum and maximum of nums.
Apply Euclid: while b, set a, b = b, a % b.
Return a.
gotcha: The learner's descending trial loop is O(min) which is fine here but Euclid or math.gcd is the standard, and the answer is at least 1 since all values are positive.

trigger: You need an index where the sum on the left equals the sum on the right.
key_idea: Right sum equals total - leftSum - nums[i], so one pass with a running left sum avoids building suffix arrays.
approach: Compute the total sum of nums.
Iterate with a running leftSum starting at 0.
Compute rightSum as total - leftSum - nums[i].
Return i when leftSum equals rightSum.
Add nums[i] to leftSum; return -1 if none found.
gotcha: Check equality before adding nums[i] to leftSum, and index 0 counts with an empty left side.

trigger: Local minima and maxima in a linked list require looking at previous, current, and next nodes at once.
key_idea: Walk three pointers and record the index of each critical point; max distance is last minus first, min distance is the smallest gap between consecutive ones.
approach: Return [-1,-1] if the list has fewer than 3 nodes.
Walk prev, curr, next together tracking the 1-based index of curr.
Append the index when curr is strictly above or below both neighbors.
If fewer than 2 critical points, return [-1,-1].
Compute min of consecutive gaps and last minus first.

complexity.space: O(n) for indices, O(1) if tracking first, last, and previous only

gotcha: Comparisons must be strict, and the head and tail can never be critical points because they lack a neighbor.

trigger: A robot walks around the border of a grid with huge step counts, so simulate positions modulo the perimeter.
key_idea: The robot only ever traverses the boundary, so reduce num modulo the perimeter 2*(w+h)-4 and then step at most one loop; a full multiple of the perimeter returns to (0,0) facing South, not East.
approach: Store position, direction, and perimeter = 2w + 2h - 4.
On step, reduce num modulo perimeter; treat 0 as a full loop.
Walk one cell at a time in the current direction.
When the next cell is out of bounds, turn counterclockwise and retry.
getPos and getDir return the stored state.

complexity.time: O(perimeter) per step call, O(1) with direct arithmetic

gotcha: After a full loop the robot ends at (0,0) facing South, so num % perimeter == 0 must walk the full perimeter rather than doing nothing, except before any move where it faces East.

trigger: Elements can only be removed from either end and you must remove two specific positions with minimum deletions.
key_idea: Only three strategies exist: remove both from the front, both from the back, or one from each end; take the minimum.
approach: Find indices of the min and max elements.
Let lo be the smaller index and hi the larger.
Front only: hi + 1 deletions.
Back only: n - lo deletions.
Mixed: (lo + 1) + (n - hi); return the minimum.
gotcha: When min and max are the same element (single-element array) the answer is index + 1, and using min/max of the two indices avoids case-splitting on which comes first.

trigger: A two-player game where only divisibility by 3 matters, so reduce stones to their residues mod 3 and count them.
key_idea: Only counts of residues 0, 1, 2 matter; zeros act as turn-skippers, so parity of cnt0 decides whether Alice needs both residues present or a large imbalance between cnt1 and cnt2.
approach: Count stones by value mod 3 into cnt0, cnt1, cnt2.
If cnt0 is even, Alice wins when cnt1 >= 1 and cnt2 >= 1.
If cnt0 is odd, Alice wins when |cnt1 - cnt2| > 2.
Return the boolean.
gotcha: Bob wins if stones run out, so Alice cannot simply stall; with odd cnt0 the zero flips who gets stuck, requiring an imbalance of at least 3.

trigger: A linked list is segmented by sentinel zero nodes and each segment must collapse into one node.
key_idea: Reuse the first node of each segment as the merged node: sum the segment values into it, then link it directly to the first node of the next segment, skipping the zero.
approach: Start at head.next as both the segment holder and scanner.
Accumulate values until the scanner hits a zero.
Store the sum in the holder node.
Advance the scanner past the zero and link holder.next to it.
Move holder to that node; return head.next when done.
gotcha: The list begins and ends with 0, so start from head.next and stop when the scanner becomes None, otherwise you read val on None.

trigger: Two lists of key-value pairs must be combined by key with values summed and output sorted.
key_idea: A dictionary keyed by value accumulates weights from both lists; sort the items at the end.
approach: Create a defaultdict of ints.
Add each weight from items1 and items2 to its value key.
Convert entries to [value, weight] lists.
Sort by value and return.
gotcha: Output must be sorted by value, so do not rely on dict insertion order.

trigger: Build the largest number from digit counts with a symmetric structure, which calls for greedy placement from 9 down.
key_idea: Pairs of a digit go on both sides, placed from 9 to 0 for maximum value; the single largest leftover digit goes in the middle, and zeros cannot lead.
approach: Count digit frequencies.
For digits 9 down to 0, append count // 2 copies to the left half.
Skip zeros if the left half is still empty.
Remember the first digit with an odd count as the middle.
Return left + middle + reversed left, or "0" if empty.
gotcha: Inputs like "00009" must return "9" and "000" must return "0", so handle leading-zero pairs and the all-empty case.

trigger: An operation removes the closest character to the left, which is exactly stack pop semantics.
key_idea: Push non-star characters; a star pops the most recently pushed character.
approach: Iterate over the string.
Push regular characters onto a stack.
On a star, pop the stack.
Join the stack into the result.
gotcha: Build the result with join on a list rather than repeated string concatenation to stay linear.

trigger: Remove every element that has a greater element somewhere to its right, which is the classic next-greater-element stack question.
key_idea: Maintain a stack of nodes with non-increasing values; when a larger node arrives, pop everything smaller since those nodes must be removed, then relink the stack top to the new node.
approach: Walk the list with a stack of nodes.
While the stack top's value is less than curr.val, pop it.
If the stack is nonempty, set top.next to curr.
Push curr and advance.
Return the bottom of the stack as the new head.
gotcha: Equal values must be kept, so pop on strictly less; alternatively reverse the list, keep a running max, then reverse back for O(1) space.

trigger: Minimize the maximum value subject to counting constraints, and feasibility of a candidate is monotonic, so binary search on the answer.
key_idea: For a candidate x, numbers not divisible by d1 are x - x//d1, not divisible by d2 are x - x//d2, and not divisible by either are x - x//lcm; check all three counts are enough.
approach: Compute lcm of divisor1 and divisor2.
Binary search x between cnt1 + cnt2 and a safe upper bound.
Feasible if x - x//d1 >= cnt1, x - x//d2 >= cnt2, x - x//lcm >= cnt1 + cnt2.
Move high down when feasible, low up otherwise.
Return low.
gotcha: Checking only the two individual conditions is not enough; the combined lcm condition prevents both arrays from claiming the same numbers.

trigger: A sorted array where you want counts of values below or above a threshold, which is a lower-bound and upper-bound search.
key_idea: Find the first index with value >= 0 (count of negatives) and the first index with value > 0 (positives are n minus that).
approach: Binary search for the first index where nums[mid] >= 0; that is neg.
Binary search for the first index where nums[mid] > 0.
Positives = n - that index.
Return max(neg, pos).
gotcha: Zeros are neither positive nor negative, so use two different boundaries (>= 0 and > 0) rather than one, and initialize the boundary to n for the all-negative case.

trigger: Two sorted arrays and you want the smallest shared element, which is a merge-style walk.
key_idea: Advance the pointer of whichever array has the smaller current value; the first equal pair is the minimum common value.
approach: Start pointers i and j at 0.
If nums1[i] < nums2[j], advance i; if greater, advance j.
On equality return that value.
Return -1 if either pointer runs off the end.
gotcha: Since both arrays are sorted, the first match found is automatically the minimum; no need to scan all matches.

trigger: Repeatedly pick the current maximum and replace it with a reduced value k times.
key_idea: A max-heap (negated values in Python) gives the largest pile in O(log n) per round.
approach: Build a max-heap by negating all gift counts.
Repeat k times: pop the max, take floor of its square root, push it back.
Return the negated sum of the heap.
gotcha: Python's heapq is a min-heap, so negate on push and pop, and use integer square root (isqrt) to avoid float rounding issues.

trigger: Each answer depends on the sum of everything to the left and everything to the right of an index.
key_idea: Build prefix sums from the left and suffix sums from the right, or use a running left sum with rightSum = total - leftSum - nums[i].
approach: Compute the total sum of nums.
Iterate with a running leftSum.
Compute rightSum = total - leftSum - nums[i].
Append |leftSum - rightSum|.
Add nums[i] to leftSum.
gotcha: The learner's prefix/suffix arrays are fine, but be careful with negative-index arithmetic in the suffix loop; the single-pass total-minus-left version is easier to get right.

trigger: Scan each row of a binary matrix and report the best row by a simple count.
key_idea: Sum each row (ones count) and keep the first row that achieves a strictly larger count.
approach: Track best index and best count starting at 0.
For each row, count its ones with sum.
Update only when the count is strictly greater.
Return [best index, best count].
gotcha: Ties must pick the smallest row index, so use strict > and not >= when updating.

trigger: Break a string into dictionary words minimizing leftovers, a word-break style DP over start indices.
key_idea: dp[i] is the minimum extra characters in s[i:]; either skip s[i] as extra (1 + dp[i+1]) or match a dictionary word starting at i and jump to its end; a trie prunes word matching.
approach: Insert all dictionary words into a trie.
Define dfs(i) with memo, base dp[len(s)] = 0.
Start with res = 1 + dfs(i + 1) for skipping s[i].
Walk the trie from i; at each word end take min with dfs(j + 1).
Break when the trie has no child; return dfs(0).

complexity.time: O(n * L) with a trie where L is max word length, O(n^2 + total dict chars) with a set

gotcha: Without a trie or a hash set, checking every substring against the dictionary list is too slow; and forgetting the skip option leaves no answer when no word matches.

trigger: Count subarrays where max minus min stays within a bound, which needs window min and max in O(1).
key_idea: Keep two monotonic deques for the window min and max; shrink from the left while max - min > 2, and every valid window ending at r adds r - l + 1 subarrays.
approach: For each r, pop from the min-deque while its back is >= nums[r].
Pop from the max-deque while its back is <= nums[r]; push r to both.
While front max minus front min > 2, advance l.
Drop deque fronts whose index is now below l.
Add r - l + 1 to the answer.
gotcha: Store indices, not values, in the deques so you can evict entries that fall out of the window.

trigger: Only one class of characters must be reordered while others stay fixed; extract, sort, and refill.
key_idea: Collect vowels, sort them by ASCII (uppercase before lowercase), then walk the string writing the next sorted vowel into each vowel slot.
approach: Collect all vowels from s into a list.
Sort that list.
Iterate s, copying consonants unchanged.
At each vowel position, write the next sorted vowel.
Join and return.

complexity.time: O(n log n), or O(n) with counting sort over 10 vowels

gotcha: Uppercase vowels sort before lowercase by ASCII, so the fixed order is AEIOUaeiou, not case-insensitive alphabetical.

trigger: Buying item i unlocks the next i items free, so the choice of the next purchase ranges over a window, a DP with range-minimum.
key_idea: dp[i] = prices[i-1] + min(dp[j]) for j in [i+1, 2i+1] (1-indexed); a monotonic deque gives that window minimum in amortized O(1) as i moves backward.
approach: Work backward from i = n to 1 with dp[n+1] = 0.
Pop deque back while its dp value >= dp[i+1], then push i+1.
Pop deque front while its index exceeds 2i + 1.
If 2i >= n, dp[i] = prices[i-1]; else add dp[front].
Return dp[1].
gotcha: Buying fruit i means you must still pay for it even if it was free; the window [i+1, 2i+1] must include 2i+1 because the next purchase can be the first fruit after the free run.

trigger: Longest contiguous subarray where every element's frequency is bounded, a classic variable-size window.
key_idea: Only the newly added element can break the constraint, so shrink from the left until its frequency drops to k.
approach: Expand r and increment freq[nums[r]].
While freq[nums[r]] > k, decrement freq[nums[l]] and advance l.
Update the best length with r - l + 1.
Return the best length.
gotcha: Check only the frequency of the element just added; checking every key in the map makes each step O(n).

trigger: Partition into fixed-size groups minimizing spread within each group; sorting and taking consecutive chunks is optimal.
key_idea: After sorting, consecutive triples have the smallest possible spread, so if any sorted triple has nums[i+2] - nums[i] > k, no valid partition exists.
approach: Sort nums.
Step through in chunks of 3.
If nums[i+2] - nums[i] > k, return [].
Otherwise append the triple.
Return the list of triples.
gotcha: Only the first and last of each sorted triple need comparing; the middle element is automatically within range.

trigger: Find a run of consecutive values at the array start, then search for a missing value at or above a threshold.
key_idea: Sum the longest prefix where each element is previous + 1, then put nums in a set and increment the candidate until it is not present.
approach: Start total at nums[0].
Add nums[i] while nums[i] == nums[i-1] + 1; break otherwise.
Convert nums to a set.
While total is in the set, increment total.
Return total.
gotcha: The prefix always includes nums[0] even if nums[1] breaks the sequence, and the missing value can equal the sum itself.

trigger: The rules describe exactly how each element is placed based on the current tails of two lists; just simulate.
key_idea: Seed arr1 with nums[0] and arr2 with nums[1], then append each following element to whichever array has the larger last element.
approach: Initialize arr1 = [nums[0]] and arr2 = [nums[1]].
For each remaining element, compare arr1[-1] and arr2[-1].
Append to arr1 if its last is greater, else arr2.
Return arr1 + arr2.
gotcha: The comparison is strictly greater for arr1, so ties go to arr2 (though values are distinct here).

trigger: Minimize the number of containers needed for a total amount; always pick the largest containers first.
key_idea: Packs can be split across boxes, so only the total apple count matters; sort capacities descending and take boxes until the running capacity covers the total.
approach: Sum all apples.
Sort capacities in descending order.
Accumulate capacities one by one.
Return the count as soon as the accumulated capacity >= total.
gotcha: Do not try to fit packs individually; the note that packs may be split means bin-packing is unnecessary.

trigger: Longest substring where each character appears at most a fixed number of times, a frequency-bounded window.
key_idea: Grow the window, and whenever the newly added character exceeds two occurrences, shrink from the left until it is back to two.
approach: Expand r and increment freq[s[r]].
While freq[s[r]] > 2, decrement freq[s[l]] and advance l.
Track the maximum r - l + 1.
Return the maximum.
gotcha: Same template as at-most-k-frequency with k = 2; only the just-added character can violate the bound.

trigger: Search for the smallest number at or above n meeting a digit condition when a nearby answer is guaranteed.
key_idea: Within any 10 consecutive integers one ends in 0, whose digit product is 0 and divisible by anything, so brute force at most 10 candidates.
approach: Loop i from n to n + 9.
Compute the product of the digits of i.
Return i when the product is divisible by t.
gotcha: A digit product of 0 counts as divisible by t, which is why the search is bounded to 10 steps.

trigger: Maximize a product of two digits from a number; you just need the two largest digits.
key_idea: Track the largest and second largest digits in one pass, allowing repeats of the same digit value.
approach: Iterate the digits of n as a string.
If digit >= n1, shift n1 into n2 and set n1 to the digit.
Else if digit > n2, set n2 to the digit.
Return n1 * n2.
gotcha: Use >= when updating the top so a repeated max digit correctly fills both slots (e.g. 99 gives 81).

trigger: Compute digit sum and digit product of a number and test a divisibility condition.
key_idea: Peel digits with mod 10 and integer division, accumulating sum and product, then check n mod (sum + product).
approach: Save a copy of n.
While n > 0, take n % 10 into sum and product; divide n by 10.
Return original % (sum + product) == 0.
gotcha: Product starts at 1, not 0, and remember to keep the original n before destroying it in the loop.

trigger: GCD of two closed-form sums, which simplifies algebraically instead of computing.
key_idea: The first n odd numbers sum to n^2 and the first n even numbers sum to n(n+1); since gcd(n, n+1) = 1, gcd(n^2, n^2 + n) = n.
approach: Recall sumOdd = n^2 and sumEven = n(n+1).
Note gcd(n, n+1) = 1.
Return n.
gotcha: Computing the sums and calling gcd also works, but recognizing the formula avoids any loop.

trigger: Reach step n with jumps of 1, 2, or 3 and additive costs; minimum cost to reach each step depends on the previous three.
key_idea: dp[i] = costs[i-1] + min(dp[i-1] + 1, dp[i-2] + 4, dp[i-3] + 9) since jump cost is the square of the jump length.
approach: Set dp[0] = 0.
For i from 1 to n, start with dp[i-1] + costs[i-1] + 1.
Take min with dp[i-2] + costs[i-1] + 4 if i >= 2.
Take min with dp[i-3] + costs[i-1] + 9 if i >= 3.
Return dp[n].

complexity.space: O(n), or O(1) keeping the last three

gotcha: costs is 1-indexed, so step i uses costs[i-1], and the jump penalty depends on distance, not on the destination alone.

trigger: Longest subsequence with a XOR property; removing one element from the full set changes the XOR, so check the whole array first.
key_idea: If the XOR of everything is non-zero, take all n; otherwise dropping any one non-zero element makes the XOR non-zero, giving n - 1, unless all elements are 0.
approach: XOR all elements and note whether any element is non-zero.
If total XOR != 0, return n.
If all elements are 0, return 0.
Otherwise return n - 1.
gotcha: Removing a zero element does not change the XOR, so the n - 1 case requires at least one non-zero element to remove.

trigger: Find the smallest value of a simple arithmetic form that is absent from an array.
key_idea: Put nums in a set and test multiples of k in increasing order; the answer is at most k * (n + 1).
approach: Convert nums to a set.
For i from 1 upward, compute k * i.
Return the first multiple not in the set.
gotcha: Since only n values can block multiples, the loop bound n + 1 always suffices; a hardcoded 105 works only because constraints are small.

trigger: Filter digits of a number, rebuild a new number, and combine with its digit sum.
key_idea: Walk the digits as a string, keeping non-zero ones for both the concatenation and the running sum, then multiply.
approach: Convert n to a string.
For each non-zero digit, append it to a result string and add to the sum.
If no digits remain, return 0.
Return int(result) * sum.
gotcha: If every digit is zero, x = 0 and the answer is 0; guard against int("").

trigger: Reverse each of several equal-length contiguous blocks in place.
key_idea: Compute the block size n / k, then reverse each block with a left and right pointer swapping inward.
approach: Compute block size = n // k.
For each block i, set l = i * size and r = l + size - 1.
Swap nums[l] and nums[r], moving pointers inward while l < r.
Return nums.
gotcha: The block length is n / k (k blocks), not k; mixing those up reverses the wrong ranges.

trigger: Asked whether some construction is always possible; check parity reasoning before coding.
key_idea: Any element can be replaced by a difference with another element, and it is always possible to make every entry the same parity, so the answer is always true.
approach: Consider parities: odd - odd and even - even are even, odd - even is odd.
Argue every index can be made even (or all odd) by choosing j appropriately.
Return True.
gotcha: Do not brute force; the trap is spending time on cases when the parity argument shows it is always achievable.

trigger: Each index needs the prefix maximum and the suffix minimum, so precompute one side and sweep the other.
key_idea: Build a suffix-min array right to left, then sweep left to right maintaining a running prefix max and return the first index where prefixMax - suffixMin <= k.
approach: Compute suffix_min[i] = min(nums[i:]) by scanning from the right.
Sweep left with a running prefix max.
Return i when prefix max - suffix_min[i] <= k.
Return -1 if none.
gotcha: Both ranges include index i itself, so the prefix max must be updated before the comparison and suffix_min[i] includes nums[i].

trigger: Compute a per-number digit statistic and sum the numbers that tie for the maximum.
key_idea: Compute each number's digit range in one pass; reset the sum when a strictly larger range appears and add to it on ties.
approach: For each number, extract its digits.
Compute range = max digit - min digit.
If range beats the best, set best and reset sum to this number.
If it ties the best, add the number to the sum.
Return the sum.
gotcha: Initialize max range so that single-digit numbers (range 0) still count; starting max_diff at 0 with an elif for ties handles that.
